A compote is a dish of fruit that has been gently cooked in a sweetened liquid — typically a simple syrup made of sugar and water. The goal is to soften the fruit and surround it with a light, flavourful sauce, while still keeping the fruit pieces recognisable and intact (not mashed or dissolved).

Think of it as fruit that has been bathed in warm sweetness until tender.
What it looks like

A compote typically looks like a bowl of soft, glistening fruit sitting in a thin, syrupy liquid. The fruit pieces are whole or roughly chopped — you can still see what fruit it is. The liquid around it is not thick like jam; it's closer to a light, slightly sweet sauce.
How it's made

You take fruit, place it in a pot with sugar (and usually water), and let it simmer gently on low heat for a short time — anywhere from a few minutes to around half an hour, depending on the fruit. This is the key word: simmered, not boiled aggressively. The gentleness is deliberate, so the fruit softens but doesn't fall apart completely.

Common additions to the cooking liquid include:

  • Spices like cinnamon, cloves, vanilla, or cardamom
  • A splash of wine (red or white), fruit juice, or even liqueur
  • A strip of lemon or orange peel, for brightness

These additions give the compote its character — a plain compote can be simple and clean, or richly spiced and aromatic.
What fruits are used

Almost any fruit can be made into a compote. The most common ones include:

  • Stone fruits — peaches, plums, cherries, apricots
  • Berries — strawberries, blueberries, raspberries, blackberries
  • Pome fruits — apples, pears
  • Dried fruits — prunes, dried figs, dried apricots, raisins (these are especially popular in winter compotes, since they rehydrate beautifully in the syrup)

You can also mix multiple fruits together. A mixed-berry compote or a pear-and-cinnamon compote are classics.
Temperature: warm or cold?

A compote can be served either warm (straight from the pot, still slightly steaming) or cold (chilled in the fridge). Both are completely normal. Warm compote feels cosy and comforting; cold compote feels refreshing. The choice usually depends on what it's being paired with.
How it's eaten

A compote is rarely eaten on its own as a standalone dish (though it can be). More often, it's used with something else, as an accompaniment or topping:

  • Spooned over vanilla ice cream or gelato
  • Dolloped onto plain yoghurt or Greek yoghurt
  • Served alongside pancakes, waffles, or crêpes
  • Layered in parfaits or trifles
  • Paired with cheesecake, panna cotta, or custard
  • Served as a side to cheese (brie with berry compote is a classic pairing)
  • In more elegant plating, used as a sauce or garnish on a dessert plate

In European cuisines — particularly French — compote also appears alongside savoury dishes. A rich duck breast or pork tenderloin might be served with a cherry compote or a plum compote, where the sweetness and acidity of the fruit cut through the fattiness of the meat. So while compote is mostly associated with sweet contexts, it isn't exclusively a dessert item.
How compote differs from similar things
This is where many people get confused, so it's worth being precise:
Compote vs. Jam/Preserve:

Jam is cooked for a long time at high heat with a large amount of sugar until it gels and becomes spreadable and shelf-stable. It's made for preservation — it can last months. Compote is cooked briefly, uses much less sugar, doesn't gel, and has a shorter life (a few days to a week in the fridge). The fruit in jam is usually completely broken down; in compote, it holds its shape.
Compote vs. Fruit sauce (like applesauce):

A fruit sauce is usually fully smooth — the fruit is cooked down and often blended or mashed into a uniform consistency. Compote keeps visible, identifiable pieces of fruit. If you look at a compote, you can see the individual strawberries or pear chunks. A sauce has no such distinction.
Compote vs. Coulis:
A coulis is a strained fruit purée — smooth, silky, no bits. A compote is chunky and syrupy.
Compote vs. Chutney:

Chutney is a condiment of South Asian origin that involves cooking fruit (often with onions and vinegar) to a thick, complex, often tangy-sweet-spicy result. It's more assertively flavoured, more acidic, and has a very different character. Compote is simpler and more delicate.
The secondary meaning: a piece of dishware

Less commonly today, "compote" also refers to a specific type of serving dish — a wide, shallow bowl mounted on a tall, decorative stem or pedestal (like a footed bowl). Historically, these elegant dishes were used to serve the fruit compote at the table, and over time the name of the dish became the name of the food served in it. You may still encounter this meaning in antique or formal dining contexts: "a silver compote on the sideboard" means the bowl, not the food.
The one-sentence summary

A compote is soft, lightly sweetened fruit cooked gently in a sugar syrup — often spiced or flavoured — and served warm or cold as a topping, side, or simple dessert, with the fruit pieces remaining intact in their surrounding syrup.
